title: Floss one tooth
hookLine: starting absurdly small helps habits begin
carry: tiny habits survive the bad days

lines: A PROMISE TOO SMALL TO BREAK.
cards: Floss one tooth. Just one. That's the instruction.
A dare from a dentist with a sense of humor, maybe. In fact it's one of B. J.

Fogg's examples of how to begin a habit, and he means it seriously: one tooth, after brushing, every night. Of course, once the floss is out and wrapped around the fingers, some nights more teeth get done.
But the promise was one, so small it was nearly impossible to break. Today's word turns that small joke into a quiet rule.

teach.b: First, too small to skip. Fogg's argument in Tiny Habits is that a new behavior should be so small it takes almost no motivation. On a tired night, a bad day, a day with no time at all, one tooth still gets done.

Big plans depend on good days; tiny ones survive bad ones. Second, the start is the hard part. Getting the floss out, sitting down on the cushion, opening the book: those first moves carry a lot of the friction.
A tiny habit is mostly a way of rehearsing the start until starting gets easy. Third, an old version of the idea.

teach.h: A TOWER FROM A HEAP OF EARTH.
teach.b: The Tao Te Ching, in its sixty-fourth chapter, as James Legge translated it, says that a tree too big to wrap your arms around grew from a tiny sprout, a tower of nine stories rose from a small heap of earth, and a journey of a thousand li began with a single step.

The same chapter advises dealing with things before they grow. Lao Tzu, as tradition names the author, and a Stanford researcher, far apart in every way, both put the weight on the small beginning. Fourth, grow it later.
Tiny isn't the goal; it's the doorway. Fogg says that once a habit is rooted, it can grow on its own, and the longer sit comes as a bonus, not a requirement. Only the floor stays tiny.
Some days thirty seconds will turn into ten minutes. Some days it will stay thirty seconds. Both days, the habit holds.

how: People using the Tiny Habits approach shrink a new habit to a version that takes seconds, like flossing one tooth or one breath of meditation, and let it grow on its own once it's rooted.

o: begin a habit so small it's nearly impossible to skip
keep a habit small forever so it never grows

p: rose from a small heap of earth

s: Fogg means the one-tooth example as a joke
it sounds like one, but he means it seriously: a promise too small to break.
the Tao Te Ching says a journey of a thousand li began with a single step
chapter sixty-four, alongside the tree from a sprout and the tower from a heap of earth.
a tiny habit only counts if it grows bigger
the floor stays tiny. thirty seconds counts, even on days it stays thirty seconds.

games.q: you want to start meditating daily. what's your first-week plan?
o: thirty minutes every morning, no exceptions.
thirty seconds after your morning coffee.
wait until you have a free weekend to start properly.
games.why: start tiny. a promise that small survives bad days, and it rehearses the start until starting gets easy.

practice: Think of a practice you'd like to keep, and ask what its thirty-second version is: three slow breaths, one line read, a look at the sky.
Now do it, thirty seconds of just breathing, nothing else expected, and notice how little it asks. If the breath wants to keep going after that, let it, as a bonus, not a requirement.

wordCard.voice: Start tiny. Begin a habit so small it's nearly impossible to skip, and let it grow later. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: tiny habits survive the bad days. Thirty seconds on the cushion counts. Rest well.
